title: Water
summary: Where it comes from, the forms it takes, and what it does for life and human society.

nodes.summary: The subject root — an overview node with no single claim of its own.
Water arrived from space and outgassed from Earth's own interior — two sources, not one.
Solid, liquid, vapor — and the phase changes between them drive weather and climate.
Every known biological process runs on water as solvent, medium, or reactant.
Drinking, growing food, making power, running industry — human society is built on reliable access.
Scarcity and shared rivers turn water into a source of leverage and conflict between people and states.
Water carries ritual and symbolic weight across nearly every human culture and religion.
Water ice existed in the cloud of gas and dust that formed the solar system; comets and water-rich asteroids delivered much of it to the young Earth.

sources.title: NASA — Where did Earth's water come from?

nodes.summary: Volcanic outgassing released water vapor trapped in the young planet's rock, which condensed as the surface cooled.
Water's asymmetric shape leaves it electrically polar, which is the root cause of nearly every unusual property it has.

sources.title: USGS — Water Science School: Water Properties

nodes.summary: Polarity lets water dissolve more substances than any other common liquid — which is why it carries nutrients, minerals and pollutants alike.
Water is one of very few substances less dense as a solid than a liquid — so lakes freeze from the top down and life survives beneath.
Evaporation, transport, condensation and precipitation move water continuously between ocean, air and land.
Cells are mostly water; it is the solvent every metabolic reaction runs in and a reactant in many of them.
Rivers, lakes and wetlands hold a disproportionate share of biodiversity relative to the tiny fraction of Earth's water they contain.
Oceans store and redistribute heat, and water vapor is the atmosphere's strongest greenhouse gas — water is the climate system's working fluid.
Safe drinking water and sanitation are the single largest historical driver of falling mortality; billions still lack reliable access.
Irrigation accounts for roughly 70% of global freshwater withdrawals — food is where most water actually goes.
Hydroelectric dams, and the cooling water that thermal and nuclear plants depend on, tie the energy system directly to water availability.
Navigable water was the cheapest way to move goods for most of history, and still carries the large majority of world trade by volume.
Nearly every early urban civilization formed on a river system — settlement patterns are water patterns.
Demand growth, depletion of aquifers and shifting rainfall are pushing more regions into chronic water stress.
Most large river basins cross a border, so upstream decisions about dams and diversions become foreign policy.
Water rights regimes — riparian, prior appropriation, customary, market-traded — decide who gets water when there isn't enough for everyone.
A dam is both an engineering object and a lever: it stores, withholds and releases on someone's schedule.
Washing, immersion and blessing with water appear independently across religions as the standard grammar of purification.
Specific rivers, springs and wells are treated as holy or living entities — some now hold legal personhood.
Flow, depth, currents, drowning, source — water supplies a large share of the metaphors humans use for time, emotion and change.
